beats.caption: May 23, 1967. The three radar sites guarding America from Soviet missiles go dark — all at the same second.
In Cold War doctrine, jamming meant one thing: Soviet attack was imminent. Nuclear-armed bombers were moved to ready-to-launch.
Days earlier, a vast sunspot group had rotated onto the Sun. On May 21 and 23 it erupted — flares, then the century's biggest radio burst.
At Ent Air Force Base, Colorado, forecaster Arnold Snyder got the panicked call. His answer: 'Yes — half the sun has blown away.'
Forecasters confirmed all three radar sites sat in daylight. As the Sun's burst faded, the 'jamming' faded with it. The launch order never came.
The near-war stayed secret for half a century — until 2016, when a declassified study named the culprit: the May 1967 Great Storm.
Quebec went dark in 1989. Earth missed a Carrington-class blast by days in 2012. We just passed solar maximum. The Sun never demobilized.
